questions.q: What makes a warp's global memory access 'coalesced'?
options: Each thread in the warp accesses a different bank of shared memory
The 32 threads access consecutive, aligned addresses that combine into a small number of wide memory transactions
The kernel uses double-precision floating point
The warp size is reduced to 16 threads
questions.explain: Coalescing happens when a warp's threads access consecutive, aligned addresses, letting the memory controller satisfy the whole warp with few wide transactions.

questions.q: Why does a strided access pattern like `in[i * stride]` hurt performance?
options: It requires double the arithmetic operations
It scatters each thread's address, forcing the controller to issue many more, narrower memory transactions for the same data volume
It only works with integer data types
It disables the use of shared memory entirely
questions.explain: A strided pattern spaces out the addresses each thread accesses, breaking coalescing and forcing more transactions to move the same number of bytes.

questions.q: Why does structure-of-arrays (SoA) layout typically coalesce better than array-of-structures (AoS) for single-field access?
options: SoA uses less total memory than AoS
SoA stores each field contiguously, so accessing one field per thread keeps addresses close together; AoS spaces them apart by the size of the whole struct
SoA automatically runs on Tensor Cores
AoS cannot be stored in global memory at all
questions.explain: In AoS, reading just one field skips over the other fields of each record, spacing addresses apart. SoA keeps each field in its own array, so single-field access stays tightly packed.

questions.q: A kernel reads the same total number of bytes whether accessed in a coalesced or scattered pattern. What changes between the two?
options: Nothing — total bytes requested is all that determines performance
The effective bandwidth utilized can differ by an order of magnitude, even though total bytes requested is the same
The kernel's arithmetic intensity increases with scattering
Scattered access always runs faster because it uses more SMs
questions.explain: Pattern, not just volume, determines how many transactions are needed. Scattered access can require far more transactions for the same byte count, tanking effective bandwidth.

questions.q: What is a common warning sign of an uncoalesced memory access in kernel code?
options: The kernel uses `threadIdx.x` directly as an index
The index into a global memory array is computed with a multiply by a stride or via an indirection like `index_array[i]`
The kernel declares a `__shared__` array
The kernel launches with more than 1024 threads per block
questions.explain: An index built from a multiply-by-stride or an indirect lookup, instead of a plain per-thread index, is the classic fingerprint of a strided, uncoalesced access pattern.
